title: Memory fragmentation & OOM: root cause notes (cudaMalloc, allocator behavior, workspace sizing)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures root-cause investigation notes for recurring GPU OOMs we've seen in the serving runtime. Symptoms are intermittent OOMs on heavy inference workloads (long sequences + batching) even when aggregate live allocation appears below device capacity. We observed workloads that previously ran fine now fail after several minutes under steady traffic.

High-level hypothesis:
- Memory fragmentation in the device allocator + transient large workspace requests (cuDNN/cuBLAS) cause situation where there is no contiguous block large enough for a subsequent allocation (cudaMalloc), producing OOM despite there being enough total free bytes.
- The runtime's allocation pattern (many short-lived small allocations interleaved with occasional large workspace allocations) exacerbates fragmentation.
- CUDA driver allocation caching and the behavior of the allocator we use (custom arena vs pytorch caching allocator) interact poorly with cudaMalloc/cudaFreeAsync timing.

Key observations from profiling and traces:
- nvprof/nsys traces show repeated cudaMalloc/cudaFree pairs around heavy ops (convolutions, matmuls) with occasional spikes of cudaMalloc that take 10s-100s of ms and then fail.
- cudaMemGetInfo sampled before and after failures reports total_free that is high enough in aggregate but the largest contiguous free block is small. We capture this via a custom helper that tries to allocate decrementing sizes to approximate largest-contiguous-block.
- GPU memory usage (nvidia-smi) shows many small allocation/deallocation deltas rather than a single large free; fragmentation ratio (defined below) climbs over time for the problematic models.
- Workspaces from cuDNN/cuBLAS are non-deterministic in size depending on algorithm selection and input dims; some algos request large temporary buffers.
- When we pinned workspace size to a known upper bound (by forcing deterministic algos or preallocating a workspace), OOMs stopped for the repro workload.

Allocator behavior notes:
- CUDA default behavior: cudaMalloc triggers the driver to find a suitable free region; driver also maintains a cache of freed blocks. However, freed blocks are not guaranteed to be coalesced into large contiguous regions, especially if fragmentation occurred across different alignment boundaries.
- cudaMallocAsync (CUDA 11.2+) can reduce fragmentation because it batches frees per stream and returns memory to the driver asynchronously; but kernel and library support varies. We tested cudaMallocAsync in a small repro and saw fewer spikes, but not a complete fix for our pattern because third-party libs (some custom fused kernels) still use cudaMalloc.
- PyTorch caching allocator (if used) pools allocations by size class which mitigates small allocation fragmentation but can worsen large contiguous allocation failures if the pool is full of small blocks. Also note env var PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb can change behavior; experimenting with this helped in a few cases.
- Our custom arena allocator uses multiple arenas (per-stream) which reduces lock contention but increases fragmentation across arenas when large allocations cross arena boundaries.

Repro steps (short):
1) Start model server with heavy synthetic traffic (sequence length 4096, batch size variable 1-8, concurrent requests 32).
2) Enable allocation tracing (env: RUNTIME_ALLOC_TRACE=1) which logs every allocation/free with size and stack hash.
3) Run nsys with memtrace enabled: nsys profile --output memtrace.nsys --trace=cuda,osrt ./run_server.sh
4) Observe OOM within ~5-30 minutes on problematic model.
5) Run helper to approximate largest free chunk: helper script attempts cudaMalloc for sizes 50%->1% of free and reports max successful.

Metrics and debug helpers we used:
- Allocation trace logs with stack hashes to map to code paths (helps identify ephemeral allocs from attention/kv cache recomputation).
- Periodic cudaMemGetInfo snapshots every second and histogram of allocation sizes.
- Largest-contiguous-free-block probe (helper) to quantify fragmentation.
- Nsight Systems timeline to correlate long cudaMalloc stalls with library calls (cudnn/cublas) and NVTX ranges.
- Env vars: PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF, CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING (for ordering), use_cuda_malloc_async flag.

Experiments and results:
- Forcing deterministic cuDNN algos (cudnnSetConvolutionMathType/deterministic config) reduced workspace variance and prevented OOM in the repro.
- Preallocating a single large workspace per model (allocated at startup) removed large transient cudaMalloc calls and eliminated fragmentation in repro. This is effective but increases baseline memory footprint.
- Switching to cudaMallocAsync reduced peak allocation latency and number of failure spikes for some workloads, but not all; third-party libs and older CUDA versions limit usefulness.
- Tweaking PyTorch allocator max_split_size_mb reduced fragmentation in workloads that used many small temporary tensors.
- Consolidating arenas (single global arena) reduced cross-arena fragmentation but increased contention and slightly higher latency at high concurrency.

Mitigations to try (ranked):
1) Short term (low risk): preallocate model workspace buffers at model init for known heavy ops; set a conservative upper bound. Document memory overhead.
2) Medium term: enable cudaMallocAsync where supported and add runtime flag to opt-in per deployment. Add an integration test to ensure dependent libraries are compatible.
3) Medium term: tune our allocator size classes and max_split_size_mb to reduce small-block waste; add periodic defragmentation policy (drain small arenas when idle).
4) Long term: implement a hybrid allocator that reserves a contiguous large region for large allocations (workspaces) and uses pooled arenas for small/medium allocations. This reduces chance of fragmentation-induced OOM.
5) Application-level: prefer deterministic/conservative algorithm selection for cuDNN/cuBLAS when running tight memory SLOs; fall back to faster algos only when there is headroom.

Operational recommendations:
- Add runtime health check that probes for largest-contiguous-free-block once per minute and alerts if contiguous free falls below a model-specific threshold for >2 minutes.
- Record allocation-stack-hash telemetry for OOM incidents to speed root cause.
- Add a canary job that runs high-memory workloads nightly to detect regressions in fragmentation behavior after runtime changes.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Quantify cost of preallocating workspaces across our model catalog (memory $$ tradeoff per model).
- Decide on default for cudaMallocAsync flag and minimum supported CUDA version for production.
- Evaluate impact of switching to single arena under peak QPS across a larger set of traffic shapes.
- Investigate third-party extensions (custom kernels) that call cudaMalloc directly — create a checklist for library authors.

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
- Sample helper to get largest contiguous free block (C++ device allocator probe): try cudaMalloc with binary search on size, starting from cudaMemGetInfo free*0.9 down to small sizes. Failing allocs should be freed immediately when used for probing.
- nsys capture: nsys profile --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --trace=cuda,osrt --output memfrag.nsys ./run_repro.sh
- envs tried: PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128, RUNTIME_USE_CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC=1, RUNTIME_ALLOC_TRACE=1

Conclusions:
- Root cause is predominantly fragmentation: large, non-deterministic workspace requests combined with a fragmented device heap.
- Short-term fixes (workspace preallocation, algorithm selection) are effective and low-risk; allocator-level improvements give better long-term reliability but require careful performance testing.
